title: Channel Tres - Breaking and Entering
summary: Channel Tres joins Simon in the studio to chat about his Australian tour, musical influences and creative process. Fresh from the release of his 2019 single 'Sexy Black Timberlake', Channel Tres reflects on his music career to date and drops some news on an upcoming release.
transcript:
Channel Tres joined Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 18 July 2019 during his second Australian visit, ahead of his EP Black Moses. They discussed touring, dance, musical influences and the characters he creates to develop his skills. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You were born in Lynwood and grew up between there and Compton. You’ve spent much of the past six months travelling and touring with artists such as Robyn, Vince Staples, Toro y Moi and Childish Gambino, who you’re touring Australia with now. You’re playing the Gershwin Room at the Espy tomorrow and Splendour in the Grass on the weekend. The last time you were here was with Ennio Styles on Stylin’, when your self-titled EP had just come out. What’s been happening since then?

Channel: The project’s coming out, it’s called Black Moses. It’s coming out on 16 August, and I’m releasing a single on 2 August entitled ‘Black Moses’. A little change-up on the BPM, so you’ll hear me go into different sounds. I’ve been getting used to the road, taking care of myself, learning and taking time to study these great people I’m going on tour with. I’m a fan of them. Just making more music, travelling and seeing the world.

Simon: When you were developing the Channel Tres project, you took some time in isolation studying in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Now you’re basing yourself in motion. What are you learning from these artists, and how are they teaching you to find balance when you’re constantly travelling?

Channel: Every artist is different. From the top of my head, Robyn was a special tour. I learnt to perform. She’s a great performer and puts on a great show. There’s a lot of emotion in her performance, and from that I learnt to connect with my songs on stage emotionally and give more to people, to the audience. Childish Gambino, I’ve seen the start of his career, back when he first started, and how he’s been consistent. It’s turned into this, and he filled up a whole arena last night. To see that from when I first saw him taught me about being consistent and persistent, never giving up and always keeping going. There’s always something new to learn and things to push forward to in music. It’s very inspiring.

Simon: Childish Gambino works across different fields. People familiar with your music know your love of different styles; you’ve said you don’t listen to music in categories. But people who haven’t seen you perform may not know that you’re a dancer too. Why is movement important to you as a musician?

Channel: I’m always sitting down playing piano or whatever I’m doing in the studio. But when you go into a dance studio, you’ve got a choreographer and you’re practising, you start to connect with your music in a different way because you move your body to certain beats. It trickles down. Now when I’m in the studio, I’m thinking about certain movements I hit. I’m like, okay, I might want to hit that, so I might put something right there. Or when I’m working with my people, I’m like, yo, do that, that’s going to go well over in the live show. It’s a different way to connect with the music more.

Simon: One of the singles from Black Moses is ‘Sexy Black Timberlake’. I presume Timberlake refers to Justin Timberlake, who’s also known as a dancer and musician. Is he influential for you?

Channel: I think he influenced everybody. I’m a big fan of early 2000s music. He was one of the ones. I think Pharrell, the Neptunes, did his first album: ‘Señorita’, all that stuff. He’s very important.

Simon: Pharrell and Chad Hugo’s productions as the Neptunes on that first record were incredible.

Simon: Black Moses is out on Godmode, like last year’s self-titled EP, which featured ‘Top Down’, ‘Jet Black’ and ‘Controller’. You hinted that this release is an opportunity to explore new ideas. Can you take us through some of the concepts?

Channel: None of it sounds like him, but I was listening to a lot of Isaac Hayes and the Shaft movie soundtrack. A lot of great tunes on there. I was watching some of his shows, and he would come out looking like a god. During that time it was really big, that was a big soundtrack. I started diving into him. The term Black Moses means a lot to me because of where I’m from. Moses led the people to the promised land, and I feel like part of what I’m doing, my journey in music, is to help my family and people in my community get to a certain place, be an example and invest back into the community. With the sounds on there, I was diving into more dance music, and I’ve got some halftime stuff on there. There’s a love letter to Detroit on there. Just getting more familiar with my voice and instrumentation and trying new things. It’s great, it’s nice.

Simon: We were talking off air about your influences, East Coast and West Coast hip-hop from the ’80s through the ’90s and 2000s. You’ve said it’s important to imbue your music with meaning. What music do you gain strength from? What records are important touchstones at the moment?

Channel: It’s a lot. From the top of my head, I’ve been listening to the Love Unlimited Orchestra, Barry White’s band. I’m going through all those. They have tracks where they remixed themes from movies and made it into some funky stuff. I like the instrumentation, it’s really important. I like how Barry White had all these musicians around him, and they’re doing what’s in his head. Even the name, Love Unlimited. That, and listening to Nate Dogg. I’m always listening to him, I love Nate Dogg. I’m still stuck on Tyler, the Creator’s new album.

Simon: Incredible record, isn’t it?

Channel: Yeah, man, it’s really good. It’s so honest, so pure. It came from an artist.

Simon: It’s another record open to different musical traditions. Before it came out, Tyler said don’t expect a rap record, because it embraces everything.

Channel: I thought that was interesting. It broke a lot of barriers for things in the atmosphere of music because people always have expectations of what they want. But we’re artists, so you have to be open to receive what maybe the universe is trying to say through that vessel or that person. You have to be open, because if you expect, you might not receive what you need from it. If you don’t like it, maybe it’s not the time for you to listen to it, but there might come a time when you do want to listen to it.

Simon: You’ve spoken about being open and receptive as an artist, but another element is remaining focused. When you were 20, you set out to play piano and produce records. You went to school, removed yourself from friends and family and devoted your attention to it. How do you keep focused and motivated when things get difficult?

Channel: Music is therapy, so that’s always my go-to, that’s what I do. It kind of works. During that time when I took all that time to develop skills, those are things I can tap into more easily, naturally, because it’s like muscle memory. I’m always making something, always on the go doing something. A lot of it is self-care, self-love. I always take time for myself. If I don’t want to do anything, I don’t do it. I try to take on projects and do things I love, and that keeps everything moving correctly. I’m not a sucker for a cheque.

Simon: One song from your earlier EP, ‘Jet Black’, was named for a superhero alter ego of yours when you were growing up. Is that right?

Channel: In Oklahoma, in college, I’d never been around that many Caucasian people before, just different people and smart people. A lot of things people were saying would fly over my head, or I’d feel left out, or like I was playing catch-up because I didn’t grow up in an environment that fostered education more. I had to study extra hard to catch up because everybody was so advanced. It made me reclusive. I’d wear the same outfit for a month because I was learning something that month, how to read music, the circle of fifths or different things. I’d wear an article of clothing every day to remind myself, and I created a character out of that. There were different characters every time. Jet Black was one of the characters, and jet black is the blackest black. I think they’ve got a new one. It’s also a magazine back in America. It’s called Jet Black. That was where Black magazines kind of started. It was a reference to that too. I’m very into characters, being something in my head and nobody would know. It’s creating personalities to get through, or if I want to achieve something. I wanted to sing and perform, so I was Bobby Brown for a month. I was watching Bobby Brown and practising. Now I have that character, so I can add something else to it. It’s a way for my mind to trick myself into doing it. I have a very vivid imagination.

Simon: When you spoke about those superpowers, one you mentioned was the power to heal through music. Have you studied healing frequencies and incorporated them into your tracks?

Channel: No, I haven’t. I know there are frequencies and different things. Sometimes I go on YouTube and listen to certain frequencies, and it calms me. That’s a study I want to get into. On further albums, maybe I may do an album and the whole album is at a certain frequency because I want to give a certain thing to people. But a lot of what I’ve been tapping into is low end. Low end is like the low chakra, and that’s the sexy vibe. That’s probably why you feel sexy in a lot of our records, because of that low frequency.

Channel: I think I’m dropping a remix of ‘Sexy Black Timberlake’ by SG Lewis on Friday. I think people are going to like this one. It’s really funky.

Simon: Stay tuned for that, it’s coming out tomorrow.
